question.:question/problem:
![](images/36/36b985c811eb28d8220017c6b7407b3a104554d785dafdb35f17553c262bdc35.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-2)$ to the point $(2,4),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-2)$ and $(2,4).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-2+t(4-(-2)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)\cdot (6t-2) \\  & =18{t}^{2}-12t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18{t}^{2}-12t+2)\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-6t+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/58/58995f1bc5b45dbe0d30a9d0cbf704d792b955e7195c0e4dc3610ddf2e576579.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-1)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,2t-1⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-1)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-1+t(1-(-1)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,2t-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)^{2}-(2t-1) \\  & =9{t}^{2}-6t+1-2t+1 \\  & =9{t}^{2}-8t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-8t+2)\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-8t+2)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/8d/8d55ece1948f9ecb7da7d489b86a297651a34f409f83ba2470f6dd06678a375e.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $3,$ traversed from the point $(0,-3)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x-y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/69/69a10b5524670d31cfc9f2982e37d58a5ee9ca39fe49f35b9dace011275a635a.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(9-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along three-quarters of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(1,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9-(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =9-9{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =9(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =9{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }9{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/b2/b21c9c11aa3320a729db0d8a71f5c89069d46527e78dfc76b47ae3925387c770.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3x+2y)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-2,2)$ to the point $(-1,1),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨t-2,\,2-t⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-2,2)$ and $(-1,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-2+t(-1-(-2))),\,(2+t(1-2))⟩ \\  & =⟨t-2,\,2-t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3x+2y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(t-2)+2(2-t) \\  & =3t-6+4-2t \\  & =t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-2)\cdot (-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2-t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/f5/f532544febd248846eede65941f4617d325d0f91fec291d2679ba28abb2fb8fc.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $2,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(0,-2),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/4d/4d02a56e1f927ccf8bd76a6fcc46dec61259649176695912865dd050657ce7f0.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a quarter of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4,$ traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(-2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/f5/f5f5b235b54d2acd20297ab365d9b93907111b3fec9a86776c28e93fdfe105ee.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(2,3),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2t,\,3t⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,0)$ and $(2,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(0+t(2-0)),\,(0+t(3-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2t)^{2}+(3t)^{2} \\  & =4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{2} \\  & =13{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}13{t}^{2}\cdot 3\,\text{d}t \\  & =39{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
